gloss_terse: purity, purifying; ritual or physical cleanness
gloss_readable: This rare noun denotes exceptional purity or the state of being purified. At Sinai, the elders saw beneath God's feet something like a pavement of sapphire stone, clear 'as the very heavens for purity' (Exodus 24:10)—an image of transcendent clarity. In Leviticus it also refers to the period of ritual purification after childbirth. The word captures both physical brightness and ceremonial cleanness.

senses.1: The single occurrence in Exodus 24:10 uses a prepositional phrase meaning 'for purity,' describing the brilliant clarity of the heavenly vision. The Spanish, French, and German translations all preserve the sense of exceptional purity or purification, reflecting both ritual and physical cleanness.

gloss_terse: clearness, luster, splendor; brilliance or shining appearance
gloss_readable: A disputed noun appearing only in Psalm 89:44 (English 89:45), referring to the removal or cessation of someone's splendor or luster. The Hebrew text is difficult, and scholars debate whether this is a variant of the purity word or a distinct term for brightness. The context describes God making the king's throne cease from its glory. Multiple ancient versions and modern translations understand this as the loss of royal splendor or brilliance.

senses.1: Found only in Psalm 89:44, this term appears in a lament over the king's humiliation. The multilingual evidence shows 'splendor' (Spanish, German) and 'purity' (French), reflecting the textual uncertainty. Most interpreters see this as the king's lost luster or royal glory being taken away.

gloss_terse: to sweep away; destroy completely with a sweeping motion
gloss_readable: A vivid verb used only in Isaiah 14:23 in God's oracle against Babylon. The Lord declares, 'I will sweep it with the besom of destruction'—using the image of a broom to convey total annihilation. The rare Pilpel verb form intensifies the action, suggesting thorough, repeated sweeping. This single occurrence makes Babylon's judgment visceral and complete, as if God will sweep away every trace of the city's arrogance.

senses.1: Isaiah 14:23 uses this verb in a dramatic pronouncement of Babylon's judgment. The consistent translation across languages as 'sweep' (English, Spanish) preserves the domestic metaphor turned apocalyptic. The imagery of sweeping with the 'besom of destruction' conveys irrevocable divine judgment through everyday language.

gloss_terse: when good, as good; temporal or comparative phrase related to goodness
gloss_readable: This is an infinitival construction appearing only in Judges 16:25, where the Philistines celebrate 'when their hearts were merry'—literally 'when good' or 'as it was good to their heart.' The phrase captures the moment when the people's spirits were high during their feast, just before they called for Samson to entertain them. The Spanish rendering 'rejoiced' interprets the emotional state, while other versions preserve the temporal sense of 'when good.'

senses.1: At the Philistine celebration for Samson's capture, this phrase marks the pivotal moment when their joy peaked. The multilingual evidence shows interpretive variation: Spanish takes it emotionally ('rejoiced'), while English and German stay closer to the temporal sense ('when good,' 'as good'). The context is the dangerous euphoria before disaster.

gloss_terse: Tob-Adonijah; personal name meaning 'good is my Lord (YHWH)'
gloss_readable: A theophoric name borne by a Levite during King Jehoshaphat's reign (2 Chronicles 17:8). The name combines the Hebrew word for 'good' with a divine title, declaring 'Good is my Lord.' However, the text is textually problematic—the Greek Septuagint shows confusion, conflating this name with others in the list. This Levite was part of a teaching mission sent throughout Judah to instruct the people in the Law.

senses.1: This proper name appears in a list of Levitical teachers commissioned by Jehoshaphat. The name's meaning ('Good is Adonijah/my Lord') is theologically significant, but the text is uncertain—the Septuagint variants suggest scribal confusion. All modern translations transliterate rather than translate this personal name, acknowledging its status as a proper noun.

gloss_terse: to be besmeared, plastered over; have the eyes or perception covered
gloss_readable: A verb appearing only in Isaiah 44:18, describing the spiritual blindness of idolaters. Their eyes 'have been besmeared' so they cannot see, and their hearts cannot understand. The passive form suggests deliberate divine judgment—God has plastered over their perception as punishment for idolatry. Some scholars see this as a variant pointing of the more common word for 'plaster' or 'coat,' intensifying the image of covered, useless eyes that cannot perceive truth.

senses.1: Isaiah 44:18 uses this verb in a devastating critique of idol-makers who cannot see their own folly. The Spanish 'closed' and English 'smeared over' both capture the idea of blocked perception. The passive voice implies divine judgment: God has sealed their eyes shut, making them incapable of recognizing the absurdity of worshiping wood.

gloss_terse: to rush, dart, swoop down; move swiftly like a bird of prey
gloss_readable: A dynamic verb used only in Job 9:26 to describe the swift passage of time. Job compares his fleeting days to 'a vulture that swoops down upon its food'—capturing the terrifying speed with which his life is disappearing. The verb conveys sudden, decisive movement, like a raptor diving from the sky. The Aramaic cognates suggest flying or rushing, making this a vivid image of predatory swiftness applied metaphorically to time's relentless advance.

senses.1: Job 9:26 uses this verb in a triple simile of speed: swift boats, an eagle, and here a swooping vulture. The Spanish 'eagle that launches itself' and English 'swooping' both capture the predatory dive. The imagery makes Job's complaint visceral—his days plunge toward death with the same inevitability as a raptor claiming its prey.

gloss_terse: fasting, hungrily; adverbial form indicating a state of abstaining from food
gloss_readable: A rare Aramaic adverb appearing only in Daniel 6:18 (English 6:19), describing how King Darius approached Daniel's den 'fasting' or 'in hunger' the morning after sealing him in with the lions. The word captures the king's anxious overnight fast, his sleepless concern for Daniel expressed through abstinence from food. The feminine ending serves as an adverbial marker, similar to other Semitic languages, making this a state or manner rather than a noun.

senses.1: Daniel 6:18 uses this adverb to describe Darius's emotional state after condemning Daniel to the lions. The multilingual evidence consistently shows 'fasting' or 'in hunger' (English, Spanish, French), emphasizing the king's distress. His refusal of food mirrors his refusal of sleep, both symptoms of his anguish over Daniel's fate.

gloss_terse: about a bowshot; distance measurement roughly equivalent to an arrow's range
gloss_readable: A participial construction appearing only in Genesis 21:16, measuring the distance Hagar placed between herself and her dying son Ishmael. The Hebrew literally reads 'like shooters of a bow'—a vivid, human-scale measurement. Unable to watch the child die, she sat 'about a bowshot away,' far enough not to witness his death but close enough to hear his cries. This poignant detail captures a mother's unbearable grief through the language of distance and archery.

senses.1: Genesis 21:16 uses this phrase to measure Hagar's emotional and physical distance from Ishmael's impending death. The consistent translation 'bowshot' or 'arrow's shot' across languages (English, Spanish, German) preserves the ancient measurement. The phrase makes abstract grief concrete—the specific distance a mother can bear between herself and her child's suffering.

gloss_terse: grinding mill, hand mill; domestic tool for grinding grain
gloss_readable: A masculine noun appearing only in Lamentations 5:13, describing the humiliation of young men forced to carry millstones during Jerusalem's destruction. Normally grinding was women's work, done by hand with heavy circular stones. The image of young men 'bearing the mill' captures their degradation—reduced to servile labor, carrying the implements of the most menial domestic task. This single occurrence makes the reversal of social roles a symbol of total conquest and shame.

senses.1: Lamentations 5:13 uses this term in a catalog of Jerusalem's humiliations after the Babylonian conquest. The Spanish and English both translate simply as 'mill' or 'grinding mill,' emphasizing the heavy labor involved. The forced carrying of millstones represents not just physical burden but social degradation, as young men are reduced to performing women's domestic work.

gloss_terse: grinding, milling; the sound or activity of grinding grain
gloss_readable: A feminine noun appearing only in Ecclesiastes 12:4 in the famous allegory of old age. The phrase 'when the sound of the grinding is low' depicts the fading of daily life's familiar sounds as one ages. Whether this refers literally to the quieting of millstones in a declining household or metaphorically to the weakening of bodily functions (perhaps teeth), the image is one of diminishing vitality. The grinding of grain was a constant, rhythmic soundtrack to ancient domestic life; its fading signals approaching death.

senses.1: Ecclesiastes 12:4 uses this term in a richly symbolic passage about aging and mortality. The Spanish 'milling' and English 'grinding' both preserve the sense of the mill's activity or sound growing faint. Whether literal (a household in decline) or metaphorical (the body's failing functions), the image evokes the slow silencing of life's ordinary rhythms.

gloss_terse: plaster, coating; material used to cover or whitewash a surface
gloss_readable: A noun appearing only in Ezekiel 13:12, where the prophet challenges false prophets who 'plaster' over Israel's problems with deceptive assurances. When the wall they whitewashed collapses, people will ask, 'Where is the coating you applied?' The term refers to the superficial covering that conceals structural weakness. Ezekiel's metaphor exposes how false prophecy is like poorly applied plaster—it looks good temporarily but provides no real strength and will fail catastrophically under pressure.

senses.1: Ezekiel 13:12 uses this term in an extended metaphor of false prophets as incompetent builders who whitewash a flimsy wall. The Spanish 'plaster' and French 'coating' both capture the sense of superficial covering. When judgment comes and the wall falls, the uselessness of their deceptive reassurances will be exposed—the plaster cannot hide fundamental rot.

gloss_terse: lambs, young sheep; specifically tender or nursling lambs
gloss_readable: A masculine plural noun appearing only in Isaiah 40:11 in a tender image of God as shepherd. The Lord 'will gather the lambs in his arms' and 'gently lead those that are nursing.' These are the most vulnerable members of the flock—young, dependent, needing special care. The word emphasizes their tenderness and need for protection. This single occurrence makes the image of divine care intensely pastoral and intimate, contrasting with the cosmic scale of Isaiah 40's opening verses.

senses.1: Isaiah 40:11 uses this term in one of Scripture's most beloved pastoral images, depicting God carrying lambs close to his heart. The Spanish diminutive 'little lambs' and the consistent translation across languages emphasize the animals' youth and vulnerability. The metaphor assures exiles that God will tenderly care for the weakest members of his people.

gloss_terse: in Telaim; geographic location where Saul mustered troops
gloss_readable: A place name appearing only in 1 Samuel 15:4, where King Saul gathered his army before attacking the Amalekites. The location is probably identical to 'Telem' mentioned elsewhere. The name's etymology is uncertain, possibly related to 'lambs' or 'young animals,' though this is speculative. The site served as a mustering point for military campaigns, suggesting it was large enough to assemble substantial forces. The precise location is now unknown, though it was somewhere in Judah's territory.

senses.1: This geographic name appears in the narrative of Saul's incomplete obedience regarding the Amalekites. The consistent transliteration 'Telaim' across languages (English, Spanish, French, German) indicates recognition as a proper place name. The site's function as a military assembly point suggests it was a significant location in Saul's kingdom, though its exact location is now lost.

gloss_terse: hurling, violent throwing; forceful propulsion through the air
gloss_readable: A noun appearing only in Isaiah 22:17, where the Lord warns a corrupt official that he will be 'hurled' or thrown violently. The phrase uses an intensive verbal construction with this noun: 'hurling you with a hurling, O man.' Some scholars prefer to re-divide the Hebrew words to create an absolute infinitive instead, but the traditional reading emphasizes the force and violence of divine judgment. This single occurrence makes the image of being thrown like a projectile a vivid picture of God's active removal of the unworthy.

senses.1: Isaiah 22:17 uses this term in a pronouncement of judgment against Shebna, a royal steward. The Spanish 'hurling' and the translations across languages capture the violent force of being thrown or cast away. The intensive construction ('hurling with a hurling') emphasizes the certainty and power of God's judgment—Shebna will be forcefully removed from his position.

gloss_terse: to roof, cover over; place timbers or covering over a structure
gloss_readable: A Piel verb appearing only in Nehemiah 3:15, describing the reconstruction of Jerusalem's walls. Shallum 'built and roofed' the Fountain Gate, completing the structure by adding protective covering. The verb is an Aramaic loan-word, reflecting the post-exilic context where Aramaic influence was strong. The act of roofing represents the final, protective stage of construction—not just rebuilding walls but making them functional. This single occurrence captures the thoroughness of Nehemiah's restoration project.

senses.1: Nehemiah 3:15 uses this verb in the detailed account of wall reconstruction, where different leaders took responsibility for different sections. The Spanish 'will roof it' and translations across languages indicate the final stage of construction—adding protective covering. The Aramaic loan-word reflects the linguistic context of post-exilic Judah, where reconstruction required both Hebrew identity and practical borrowing from surrounding cultures.

gloss_terse: to have shade, find shelter; be covered or protected from sun
gloss_readable: A Haphel (Aramaic Hiphil) verb appearing only in Daniel 4:12 (Aramaic 4:9), describing the beasts finding shade under Nebuchadnezzar's dream-tree. The imagery is of a tree so vast that animals shelter beneath its branches. This represents the king's empire providing protection and benefit to many peoples. The verb emphasizes the tree's function as shade-provider, making the natural world dependent on its presence. When the tree is cut down, that protective covering is lost.

senses.1: Daniel 4:12 uses this verb in the symbolic vision of a cosmic tree representing Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom. The Spanish 'sheltered themselves' and English 'found shade' both capture the sense of protective covering. The tree's shade represents the empire's benefits to subject peoples—when God cuts it down, that protection vanishes, leaving the beasts exposed.

gloss_terse: uncleanness; state of ritual or moral impurity
gloss_readable: A feminine noun appearing only in Micah 2:10, where the prophet warns that the land has become defiled. 'Arise and go, for this is no place of rest, because of uncleanness that destroys.' The term refers to ethical impurity from wrongdoing, not just ritual defilement. The land itself has been polluted by injustice and oppression, making it uninhabitable for God's people. The noun form emphasizes the settled state of corruption, not just individual acts but a condition of deep defilement requiring exile.

senses.1: Micah 2:10 uses this term in a prophetic oracle of judgment, commanding the people to leave their defiled land. The Spanish 'uncleanness' and French 'impure' both point to ethical rather than merely ritual defilement. The land's uncleanness comes from the people's oppression of the weak, making even the promised land a place from which they must flee.

gloss_terse: to be regarded as unclean, considered stupid; be stopped up or dull
gloss_readable: A disputed verb appearing only in Job 18:3 in the Niphal, where Bildad protests Job's attitude: 'Why are we regarded as unclean in your sight?' The verb's root and meaning are uncertain—it may derive from a root meaning 'stopped up' (Aramaic), or it may be a variant spelling of the word for 'unclean.' Ancient versions and modern scholars are divided. Either reading works: Job's friends feel either ceremonially degraded or intellectually dismissed as 'stupid' by Job's arguments. The context is a heated debate where respect has broken down.

senses.1: Job 18:3 uses this verb in Bildad's offended response to Job's critiques of his friends' counsel. The Spanish 'we are unclean' favors the ritual reading, while commentators also suggest 'we are regarded as stupid' or 'stopped up.' The textual uncertainty reflects the emotional heat of the debate—Job's friends feel insulted, whether ceremonially or intellectually.

gloss_terse: to soil, defile; make dirty or ritually impure
gloss_readable: A Piel verb appearing only in Song of Songs 5:3, where the beloved woman hesitates to open the door for her lover: 'I have washed my feet—how can I soil them?' The verb captures her momentary reluctance to get her clean feet dirty by walking to the door. The word is an Aramaic form used poetically, adding exotic flavor to the love poem. This single occurrence makes mundane domesticity—clean feet, reluctance to re-dirty them—part of the playful, teasing rhetoric of courtship.

senses.1: Song of Songs 5:3 uses this verb in the beloved's coy response to her lover's knocking. The Spanish 'I will soil them' and French 'would I soil them?' both capture her rhetorical question about re-dirtying her freshly washed feet. The Aramaic loan-word contributes to the Song's distinctive poetic register, mixing languages as freely as it mixes metaphors of love.

gloss_terse: to lead astray, cause to wander; make someone deviate from the right path
gloss_readable: A Hiphil verb appearing only in Ezekiel 13:10, condemning false prophets: 'They have led my people astray.' The causative form emphasizes that these prophets actively caused wandering rather than passively allowing it. The root suggests straying or deviation, both physical and spiritual. False prophecies of peace when there is no peace caused the people to wander from truth and trust in lies. This single occurrence makes prophetic deception a form of deliberate misdirection, leading the flock away from the true shepherd.

senses.1: Ezekiel 13:10 uses this verb in God's indictment of false prophets who proclaim 'Peace' when judgment is imminent. The Spanish 'made to err' and translations across languages emphasize the causative action—these prophets actively led people astray. Their lies caused spiritual wandering, making the people miss the path of repentance and walk toward destruction while believing they were safe.

gloss_terse: to load; place cargo or burdens on pack animals
gloss_readable: A Qal imperative appearing only in Genesis 45:17, where Joseph (through Pharaoh) commands his brothers to 'load your beasts' with grain and provisions for the journey back to Canaan. The verb captures the practical logistics of ancient travel—donkeys and camels bearing goods across long distances. This single occurrence makes a simple command part of the dramatic reconciliation story: the same brothers who sold Joseph now receive his abundant provision, symbolized by heavily laden animals returning to their father.

senses.1: Genesis 45:17 uses this imperative in Pharaoh's generous instructions to Joseph's brothers. The Spanish 'load' and German 'load' both preserve the straightforward command to pack their animals with Egyptian abundance. The act of loading represents the reversal of fortune—from famine to feast, from rejection to reconciliation, symbolized in beasts of burden carrying blessing back to Jacob.

gloss_terse: pierced, run through; those struck with a sword or spear
gloss_readable: A Pual participle appearing only in Isaiah 14:19, describing corpses in a mass grave: 'those pierced by the sword.' The passive form emphasizes the victims' condition rather than the act of piercing. The context is the king of Babylon's disgraceful burial, thrown out like refuse among the war-slain. The participle functions as a substantive—'the pierced ones'—making violent death into a category of person. This single occurrence captures the grim aftermath of battle through the image of bodies pierced and discarded.

senses.1: Isaiah 14:19 uses this participle in a taunt against Babylon's fallen king, denied honorable burial and cast among common war victims. The Spanish 'pierced by' and translations across languages emphasize the violent manner of death. The phrase 'those pierced with the sword' became almost formulaic for battlefield casualties, and the Babylonian king's corpse is numbered among them without distinction.

gloss_terse: tender care, dandling; the nurturing attention given to infants
gloss_readable: A plural abstract noun appearing only in Lamentations 2:20, in a horrific question about mothers eating 'the children of their tender care'—infants they have lovingly nursed and dandled. The word captures the intimate physical affection of a mother holding and bouncing her baby, making the reversal in siege conditions even more appalling. This single occurrence uses the language of gentlest nurture to intensify the horror of famine-driven cannibalism during Jerusalem's destruction.

senses.1: Lamentations 2:20 uses this term in one of Scripture's most disturbing images, asking whether women should eat babies they have tenderly cared for. The Spanish question mark and uncertain translations across languages reflect the term's rarity and the passage's difficulty. The noun 'tender care' or 'dandling' emphasizes the loving physical attention that makes the siege's outcome unbearable to contemplate.

gloss_terse: to take quick steps, trip along; walk with short, affected steps
gloss_readable: A Qal infinitive absolute appearing only in Isaiah 3:16, mocking the affected gait of Jerusalem's elite women: they 'walk along tripping' or 'taking mincing steps.' The verb captures a self-consciously dainty, attention-seeking manner of walking. Combined with other details—outstretched necks, flirting eyes, tinkling anklets—this creates a satirical portrait of vanity and self-display. This single occurrence makes an exaggerated feminine walk into a symbol of spiritual pride and coming judgment.

senses.1: Isaiah 3:16 uses this infinitive absolute in a prophetic satire of wealthy Jerusalem women's ostentatious behavior. The Spanish 'with little steps' and translations across languages capture the affected, mincing gait. The verb suggests both physical manner (short, quick steps) and moral character (vain self-display), making how one walks a revelation of inner pride deserving judgment.

gloss_terse: to be gross, become insensitive; have a heart that is fat and unresponsive
gloss_readable: A Qal perfect verb appearing only in Psalm 119:70, where the psalmist contrasts himself with the wicked: 'Their heart is gross like fat, but I delight in your law.' The verb uses the metaphor of physical fatness for spiritual insensibility—a heart so encased in fat it cannot feel or respond. The image recalls prophetic warnings about hearts becoming hardened or heavy. This single occurrence makes bodily grossness a vivid picture of moral and spiritual numbness, the opposite of the sensitive, Torah-delighting heart.

senses.1: Psalm 119:70 uses this verb in a contrast between the psalmist's responsive heart and the wicked's insensitive one. The Spanish 'became gross' and translations across languages emphasize the fat-encased, unfeeling condition. The metaphor draws on ancient physiology where the heart's literal fatness was thought to impede its function, making this a powerful image of spiritual unresponsiveness to God's word.

gloss_terse: Taphath; personal name, daughter of Solomon
gloss_readable: A feminine personal name appearing only in 1 Kings 4:11, identifying one of Solomon's daughters who married Ben-Abinadab, one of the king's district governors. The name's etymology is uncertain, though some suggest it relates to 'drops' or 'ornament.' She represents Solomon's strategic use of marriage to bind his administrative officials to the royal family. This single occurrence makes her one of the few Solomon's daughters named in Scripture, significant primarily for the political alliance her marriage created.

senses.1: This personal name appears in the list of Solomon's district governors and their connections to the royal house. The consistent transliteration 'Taphath' (English, Spanish, French, German) reflects its status as a proper name. Her marriage to Ben-Abinadab illustrates how Solomon used family ties to consolidate administrative loyalty across his kingdom.

gloss_terse: [ketiv] before, not yet; temporal adverb indicating precedence (variant spelling)
gloss_readable: This is the Ketiv (written) form appearing only in Ruth 3:14, a variant spelling of the common adverb meaning 'before' or 'not yet.' The Qere (read) form is the standard 'terem.' Boaz and Ruth rise early, 'before one could recognize another,' maintaining discretion about their nighttime encounter on the threshing floor. The variant spelling doesn't change meaning, just reflects different scribal traditions. This single occurrence shows the textual variants that preserve both written and traditional reading forms.

senses.1: Ruth 3:14 uses this variant form in the narrative of Boaz's careful protection of Ruth's reputation. The bracketed notation in translations acknowledges this is a Ketiv variant of the standard word for 'before.' The phrase 'before dawn' or 'before recognition' emphasizes the discretion both characters showed, rising early to avoid scandal before their honorable intentions could be fulfilled in marriage.

gloss_terse: to burden, load; weigh down or impose a load upon
gloss_readable: A Hiphil imperfect verb appearing only in Job 37:11, in Elihu's speech about God's control of weather: 'He loads the clouds with moisture.' The verb captures the image of clouds being burdened or weighted down with water until they release it as rain. The Aramaic root suggests toil or burden, here applied to the meteorological cycle. This single occurrence makes divine weather-control into an act of loading and unloading, as if God were a porter packing clouds with cargo they must deliver.

senses.1: Job 37:11 uses this verb in Elihu's discourse on God's majesty displayed in storms and weather. The Spanish 'loads' and translations across languages preserve the image of clouds being weighed down or burdened with moisture. The metaphor makes meteorology into logistics—God loads the clouds with water-cargo, which they transport and deliver as rain across the earth.

gloss_terse: fresh-plucked, freshly torn off; newly detached from a plant
gloss_readable: An adjective appearing only in Genesis 8:11, describing the olive leaf the dove brought back to Noah: 'a freshly plucked olive leaf.' The word emphasizes the leaf's newness—it was just picked, still green and fresh, proving vegetation had emerged from the flood waters. The Aramaic cognate suggests a fresh leaf still vital with life. This single occurrence makes botanical freshness the signal of earth's renewal, the first tangible evidence that dry land and living plants had survived the deluge.

senses.1: Genesis 8:11 uses this adjective in the famous scene of the dove returning to the ark with evidence of receding flood waters. The consistent translation 'freshly plucked' (English, Spanish, French, German) emphasizes the leaf's recent removal from a living tree. The fresh green olive leaf became an enduring symbol of peace and new life emerging from judgment.

gloss_terse: Tarpelites; ethnic or administrative group in Persian period
gloss_readable: A gentilicial or administrative term appearing only in Ezra 4:9, in a list of groups opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's temple. The identification is uncertain—some see this as an ethnic designation, others as an official title meaning something like 'beyond the river' in Persian administrative language. The Greek translations vary, suggesting ancient uncertainty about this group's identity. They were among the coalition of opponents writing to King Artaxerxes to stop the temple construction.

senses.1: Ezra 4:9 includes this term in a catalog of opposition groups petitioning the Persian king against Jerusalem's restoration. The transliterations across languages acknowledge uncertainty about whether this is an ethnic name or an official title. Some scholars connect it to Persian words meaning 'trans-river officials,' reflecting the administrative structure of the Persian Empire's western provinces.

gloss_terse: to long for, desire; have intense yearning or craving
gloss_readable: A Qal perfect verb appearing only in Psalm 119:131, where the psalmist declares passionate desire for God's commands: 'I longed for your commandments.' The verb is an Aramaic loan-word used in this late psalm to express intense yearning or craving. The image is physical—the psalmist pants or gasps with desire (the previous line), then declares this deep longing. This single occurrence makes spiritual desire as visceral as thirst or hunger, borrowing Aramaic vocabulary to intensify Hebrew devotion.

senses.1: Psalm 119:131 uses this verb in the psalmist's declaration of love for Torah. The Spanish 'yearned' and translations across languages capture the intense desire. The Aramaic loan-word adds emotional intensity to this acrostic psalm's expression of Torah devotion—the psalmist doesn't just obey or study God's commands, but longs for them with physical yearning.

gloss_terse: to be fitting, appropriate; be suitable or proper for something
gloss_readable: A Qal perfect verb appearing only in Jeremiah 10:7, in a hymnic declaration of God's uniqueness: 'Fear is fitting for you, O King of the nations.' The verb declares what is appropriate or suitable, what ought to be. The Aramaic form adds solemn weight to this rhetorical question comparing YHWH to worthless idols. This single occurrence makes fittingness or propriety a theological category—reverence for God is not just commanded but inherently appropriate, befitting his nature and status.

senses.1: Jeremiah 10:7 uses this verb in a confession of YHWH's incomparability among the gods. The Spanish 'corresponds' and translations like 'it is due' capture the sense of appropriateness or fittingness. The late Aramaic form intensifies the rhetorical force—fear of the true King is not arbitrary but intrinsically fitting, the only proper response to his majesty.

gloss_terse: the Jairite; gentilicial designation indicating clan or regional origin
gloss_readable: A gentilicial adjective appearing only in 2 Samuel 20:26, identifying Ira as 'the Jairite,' one of David's officials. The designation indicates clan or regional origin, probably from Jair or a place associated with that name. The precise reference is unclear—it may connect to the Jair who judged Israel, or to Havvoth-Jair in Gilead, or to another Jair family. This single occurrence makes Ira's clan identity part of his official title, suggesting regional or kinship ties mattered in David's administration.

senses.1: This gentilicial term appears in the list of David's officials, where Ira the Jairite is called 'a priest to David' or 'David's chief minister.' The consistent transliteration 'Jairite' (English, Spanish, French, German) indicates recognition as a clan or regional designation. The term identifies Ira by his origin, though the exact connection to other biblical Jairs remains debated.

gloss_terse: Jeatherai; personal name of a Levite ancestor
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing only in 1 Chronicles 6:21 (English 6:6), in the genealogy of the Levitical musician Asaph. The name apparently corresponds to 'Ethni' in verse 41 (English verse 26) of the same chapter, representing the same individual recorded with variant spelling. Such genealogical variations are common in Chronicles' complex family lists. This single occurrence makes Jeatherai one link in the chain connecting the post-exilic Levitical singers to their ancient priestly heritage.

senses.1: This personal name appears in the genealogical records establishing the legitimacy of post-exilic Levitical musicians. The transliterations vary, and the apparent equivalence with 'Ethni' in the parallel genealogy suggests textual variation in transmission. The name serves primarily to establish ancestral continuity for the temple musicians, linking them to pre-exilic Levitical families.

gloss_terse: to cry out shrilly, lament; make a high-pitched wailing sound
gloss_readable: A Piel consecutive imperfect verb appearing only in Judges 5:28, where Sisera's mother 'cried out shrilly' through the window, anxiously watching for her son's return from battle. The verb captures a high-pitched, penetrating sound—somewhere between calling and lamenting. The irony is devastating: she waits for a victorious return that will never come, her shrill cries anticipating the lament they should become. This single occurrence makes maternal anxiety into a sharp, piercing sound that contrasts with the battle's brutal reality.

senses.1: Judges 5:28 uses this verb in the Song of Deborah's ironic conclusion, depicting Sisera's mother waiting for a son already dead. The Spanish 'lamented' and translations capturing outcry or shrilling both fit the context. Her penetrating cry through the window embodies anxious anticipation soon to become genuine mourning, though she doesn't yet know her son lies slain by Jael's tent peg.

gloss_terse: Jabal; personal name, son of Lamech, father of tent-dwelling herdsmen
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing only in Genesis 4:20, identifying one of Lamech's sons by Adah as 'the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.' Jabal represents the origin of pastoral nomadism in the Cainite genealogy. The name may relate to the Hebrew word for 'stream' or 'watercourse,' appropriate for a founder of shepherding. This single occurrence makes Jabal the eponymous ancestor of a whole way of life—tent-dwelling, animal-herding existence that characterized much of ancient Near Eastern culture.

senses.1: Genesis 4:20 names Jabal as the founder of pastoral life in the genealogy of Cain's descendants. The consistent transliteration (with slight variations: 'Yaval,' 'Jabal') across languages reflects its status as a personal name. As 'father of those who dwell in tents,' Jabal represents the cultural origin of nomadic shepherding, one of humanity's primary economic adaptations.

gloss_terse: running sore, ulcer; a suppurating or weeping wound
gloss_readable: A feminine adjective used substantively appearing only in Leviticus 22:22, in the list of animal blemishes that disqualify sacrifices. Animals with 'a running sore' or 'weeping ulcer' cannot be offered to the Lord. The word emphasizes the active, suppurating nature of the wound—it's not healed but actively discharging. This single occurrence makes ritual purity dependent on bodily wholeness; animals with open, weeping wounds are unsuitable for holy use, even if otherwise healthy.

senses.1: Leviticus 22:22 uses this term in the catalog of disqualifying blemishes for sacrificial animals. The Spanish 'with wart' and translations like 'running sore' or 'ulcer' indicate an actively suppurating wound. The holiness code requires unblemished offerings, and weeping, open sores—like blindness, broken bones, or skin diseases—render animals ritually unsuitable for the altar.

gloss_terse: Jabneh; Philistine city conquered and demolished by Uzziah
gloss_readable: A place name appearing only in 2 Chronicles 26:6, identifying a Philistine city whose walls King Uzziah broke down during his military campaigns. The name means 'he causes to build' or 'he builds,' which is ironic given the context of demolition. The site is identified with the later Jamnia/Yavneh, which became significant in Second Temple and rabbinic Judaism. This single occurrence marks Jabneh as one of Judah's territorial gains during Uzziah's successful reign before his pride led to downfall.

senses.1: This place name appears in the account of Uzziah's military successes against the Philistines. The transliterations vary ('Jabneh,' 'Jabne'), but the site is identified with the important coastal city that later became Jamnia. Uzziah's breaking down of Jabneh's walls represents Judah's temporary expansion into Philistine territory during the 8th century BC.

gloss_terse: and Ibneiah; personal name of a Benjamite
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing only in 1 Chronicles 9:8, in the list of post-exilic Benjamite residents of Jerusalem. The name probably means 'YHWH builds' or 'YHWH builds up,' comparable to other theophoric names with the building root. The Greek textual variants show considerable confusion with this and surrounding names, suggesting manuscript difficulties in this genealogical section. This single occurrence makes Ibneiah one of the many returning exiles who resettled Jerusalem, his name testifying to faith in God's rebuilding work.

senses.1: This personal name appears in Chronicles' list of post-exilic Benjamite families living in Jerusalem. The textual variants in the Septuagint reflect the difficulty of transmitting genealogical lists accurately. The theophoric name ('YHWH builds') is theologically appropriate for the restoration period, when God's people were literally rebuilding Jerusalem and the temple after Babylonian exile.
